articles.title: Juliana Canet, influencer catalana, defiende que nunca hará contenido en castellano: “Cataluña es un país colonizado y ocupado”
articles.standfirst: La creadora de contenido abogó por la independencia durante la gala de los Premios Ondas 2026
articles.summary: La creadora de contenido abogó por la independencia durante la gala de los Premios Ondas 2026
articles.body: Juliana Canet volvió a estar en el centro de un debate lingüístico y político cuando pronunció un discurso en la ceremonia de los Premios Ondas este jueves, 26 de noviembre, en Barcelona. La presentadora utilizó el premio para el programa ‘Que no surti d’aquí’ de Catalunya Ràdio para defender el uso del catalán y su punto de vista sobre la identidad de Cataluña. La comunicadora ganó el premio a la mejor idea de radio junto a sus compañeros Roger Carandell y Marta Montaner. Pero además del reconocimiento profesional, sus palabras durante la ceremonia fueron uno de los momentos más destacados del día porque contenían muchos mensajes políticos y reivindicaciones sociales. Juliana, quien ha estado defendiendo públicamente durante años su insistencia en hablar solo catalán, no perdió la oportunidad de reiterar este mensaje. Su discurso estuvo lleno de referencias históricas y culturales, así como un mensaje explícito sobre la situación política del territorio. “Estamos contentos de haber podido hacer todo este recorrido enteramente en catalán. El idioma es el alma de un país y merece toda la atención posible, también lo dijo Mercè Rodoreda, especialmente si vives en un país como el nuestro, colonizado y ocupado durante siglos)”, dijo al público. Una posición que ha mantenido durante años. No es la primera vez que la influencer se pronuncia sobre el idioma en el que desarrolla su actividad profesional. Durante una entrevista con El Periódico ya lo dejó claro con una declaración que ahora resurge: “Nunca crearé contenido en español”. En ese momento Canet presentaba el programa de TV3 ‘Tot són problemes’ con Patrick Urbano y Serapi Soler. Desde entonces ha mantenido una línea de comunicación en la que el catalán está en el centro (intervenciones públicas así como proyectos audiovisuales y radiofónicos). En los Ondas también quiso explicar qué significado le da al uso de este idioma en el espacio público. “En este sentido, estar frente al micrófono todos los días hablando catalán pero también en tu vida diaria y aquí ahora es un acto de liberación, es una forma de decir que no es tan fácil pisotearnos”, añadió. La presentadora quiso distanciar su mensaje de cualquier lectura derrotista y terminó apelando a la continuidad histórica del idioma: “Y no lo digo victimizando o derrotistamente sino con la máxima esperanza. Ausiàs March ya hablaba catalán en el siglo XV y nosotros seguimos haciéndolo ahora. Viva Cataluña libre”.

articles.body: Tras el debate a cuatro de este jueves, 26 de noviembre, muchos los usuarios que se han pronunciado en redes sociales. El más llamativo, dada su fama, ha sido Borja Iglesias. El delantero del RC Celta ha mostrado su parecer de una forma sin precedentes: mediante carteles de publicidad. Con ellos hace público su malestar por situaciones que vive parte de la población en el día a día. Como se pueden ver en las imágenes compartidas por Borja Iglesias en su cuenta de X, recrea conversaciones entre dos personas. La primera dice lo siguiente: “Han agredido a Pablo al grito de ‘maric**”. A lo que la otra persona le contesta: “Bueno, yo soy hetero. ¿Qué hay de cenar”. En el cartel se extrae una primera conclusión: “Qué fácil sería defender solo los derechos que yo necesito, ¿verdad?”. articles.title: GTA 6 crashes into top end of music chart after its record launch
articles.summary: Several songs on the game's soundtrack have climbed the UK's singles chart.
articles.body:
Grand Theft Auto 6 has been swerving into online feeds and cultural conversations since its record-breaking launch last week.

But one area where the game is really making a dent is the world of music.

Flower In A Hurricane, the single from the game's official soundtrack album by Justice featuring Tame Impala, SZA and King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard, has climbed to number three on the UK's Official Singles Chart.

Go Easy, a new track from Dua Lipa specially recorded for the game, is the highest new entry at 21.

Seven other songs recorded for GTA 6 by artists including Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott and Morgan Wallen also placed in the top 100.

Video game music has topped the UK chart before, when Robbie Williams' It's Only Us, recorded for the FIFA 2000 soundtrack, got to number one.

Run Away With Me, a 2015 song by Carly Rae Jepsen used during a "needle drop" moment in the game's first chapter, has also seen a huge spike in listeners.

It originally peaked at number 58 in the UK 11 years ago, but has re-entered the charts at number 28.

Speaking to BBC music correspondent Mark Savage, Jepsen remembered feeling the track had "something special to it" when she recorded it.

While it's a favourite among some of the singer's most loyal fans, it has never reached the level of recognition as her hits Call Me Maybe and I Really Like You.

"It never got eyes like it's getting right now," she said.

"It's just so lovely to see that happening, it makes me believe in that special feeling that we had."

There are three elements of GTA 6's soundtrack, including an official, double-sided album containing tracks recorded for the game, and an original score composed by electronic duo Justice, due to be fully released in December.

The game also features hundreds of licensed tracks on its in-game radio stations.

Flower In A Hurricane was released as a single in October, giving it time to appear on playlists in the lead-up to the game's debut.

But Mat Ombler, head of partnerships at video game music label Laced Records, says GTA 6's impact on the charts is still impressive.

He says video game soundtracks entering the album charts "isn't unheard of" but "it's incredibly rare to see multiple tracks hitting the singles charts".

Ombler likens the spike in streams of Jepsen's track to the boost Kate Bush's Running Up That Hill got from its inclusion in Netflix hit Stranger Things.

"Both tracks are part of a huge cultural moment, but I'd argue that GTA's usage of Run Away With Me is more impactful... where the music responds according to what you're doing during a key story mission," he says.

Ombler thinks the chart impact of GTA 6 highlights "the growing importance and cultural impact of video game soundtracks as a whole".

"Over 40 million people will spend the coming weeks and months listening to more than 800 tracks featured in the in-game radio stations, possibly hundreds of times," he says.

"They'll discover new music in genres they might never have engaged with otherwise, and this music will stick with them for the rest of their lives."

Only One by New York band Fcukers appears on the official GTA 6 soundtrack and has already had more than one million streams on Spotify.

The group's singer Shanny Wise tells Newsbeat: "It was actually one of the songs we recorded when we were making our album, but it didn't end up making the album."

"We felt like the vibe of it maybe was too much of an outlier," adds bassist Jackson Walker Lewis.

"But when the GTA thing came around... I felt like it perfectly fit."

Lewis says the band didn't know they'd made the official soundtrack album until the tracklist leaked in the days leading up to the game's release.

"The one thing I'll say is, Rockstar operates very fluidly behind the scenes," says Lewis.

"They can change their mind last-minute. I think that's what makes them so good at what they do is because they have flexibility."

The electronic duo agree it was "beyond an honour" to appear alongside huge names such as pop star Dua Lipa and rapper Travis Scott.

"I mean, it's crazy and really... it blows me away," says Wise.

But, Lewis says, it's not the only thing making their big moment special.

"I think it's been a really long time since kind of globally we've had a monoculture moment that we can all share in, you know, in a positive way, in a joyful way," he says.

"Everyone across the globe is, for the most part, enjoying this game, and I just think it's a special thing to be a part of."

Steven Ellison, better known as Flying Lotus, points out the GTA series was already an established cultural phenomenon.

Millions of players heard the US producer, DJ, film-maker and rapper hosting FlyLo, one of GTA 5's in-game radio stations.

He also curated its tracklist - a job he confesses was made easier by the series' profile.

"People just wanted to have any involvement at all," he says.

"It was like: 'Who do we want? Who don't we want?' It was incredible."

He says the role gave him an opportunity to "shine a light on musicians from LA", his hometown, and the inspiration for the game's fictional location Los Santos.

It also influenced his own musical taste, he says.

"I remember when I played GTA: Vice City and it was the first time I actually listened to Africa by Toto.

"I was like: 'Man this song is awesome'. I didn't really know it before."

That curated experience, according to Ellison, is a big part of the appeal, and why the game can generate surprise hits out of neglected songs.

"It's so hard to get an experience like that nowadays with the way we listen to music and find music," he says.

"So this is kind of like that experience from back in the day where you're actually being put on to something by hanging out with people and then someone plays a track.

"It's that genuine connection that I think is possible with this."

articles.title: Christian social worker wins discrimination case over LGBT views
articles.summary: The Court of Appeal found Felix Ngole, from Barnsley, was discriminated against by his Leeds-based potential employer.
articles.body:
A company discriminated against a Christian social worker by not offering him a job because of his religious beliefs on homosexuality, the Court of Appeal has ruled.

Felix Ngole was offered a role at Touchstone in 2022, but the Leeds-based mental health charity retracted a job offer a month later after learning about news articles relating to a previous court case Ngole had been involved in.

It involved a successful legal challenge against the University of Sheffield over its decision to expel him from an MA course for social media comments Ngole made in 2015 stating "homosexuality is a sin".

Following the latest decision, Ngole said his religious beliefs did not make him a "danger to others".

Ngole, who is from Barnsley and was supported by the Christian Legal Centre, described it is an "important victory", adding: "There was no evidence whatsoever that I would treat any service user without dignity, compassion, and respect."

In written submissions, Katherine Apps KC, representing Touchstone, said Ngole showed "resistance" to attending LGBT+ awareness training and there was a "risk of complaints or claims" against the company by service users.

She said Touchstone declined to offer Ngole the job after a second interview because of a "lack of enthusiasm" for what the company "wished to see in the role, including actively promoting LGBTQI+ specific service and specifically tailoring services to the needs of LGBTQI+ service users".

After offering Ngole the role in 2022, Touchstone said his views went against its own but offered to reconsider if he assured the company his beliefs would not compromise his role.

After a second interview the company declined to offer Ngole the role, stating in a letter it felt his views could pose a "significant risk" to its users and they could find the comments "upsetting and offensive".

Bruno Quintavalle, representing Ngole, told the Court of Appeal earlier this year that making him attend a second interview meant Touchstone "imposed upon him requirements that were not imposed on anyone else".

He said this represented a "very straightforward matter of direct discrimination".

In 2024, an employment tribunal (ET) ruled Touchstone directly discriminated against Ngole by rescinding the initial job offer.

However, the ET rejected claims that requiring him to attend a second interview and not offering him the job were also discriminatory.

Ngole appealed that decision and in February the Employment Appeal Tribunal (EAT) judge found against both of the ET's decisions and sent the case back for reconsideration.

Ngole challenged that decision at the Court of Appeal in September.

By a majority ruling on Friday, the Court of Appeal upheld Ngole's challenge and dismissed Touchstone's, while also refusing the charity's bid to take the case to the Supreme Court.

In a ruling, Lady Justice Elisabeth Laing said: "Mr Ngole's 'public manifestation of his beliefs' happened long before he applied for the job.

"I cannot accept that that past public manifestation… which was lawful when made and which was no more than an accurate description of those lawful beliefs, could become 'objectionable' because of the nature of the job for which he applied."

Agreeing with the decision, Lord Justice Miles said the "only tenable conclusion" was that Touchstone was "significantly influenced" by media reporting about Ngole's views.

He said while the views "may not be generally accepted and indeed may offend many people", they were expressed in an "objectively unobjectionable manner".

articles.title: Joe Rogan says American education system is turning young people against their own country
articles.summary: Podcaster Joe Rogan says the American education system teaches kids to view the American flag as a symbol of oppression, undermining freedom's values.
articles.body: Podcaster Joe Rogan called out the American education system for turning young Americans against their country, arguing it is the world’s best bastion of freedom. Rogan released a prerecorded episode on the eve of Thanksgiving in which he spoke to retired Navy SEAL and podcaster Jocko Willink about American exceptionalism. Willink argued that the ultimate antidote to fascism and communism is to be a freedom-loving American, but Rogan warned that the country's education system is undermining those very values. "The problem today is, especially, like, young kids straight out of universities, they have actually associated the American flag with a symbol of oppression, which is so wild," Rogan said. "It's so wild because, like, the American flag means all of us. It means the American people. It means this experiment in self-government. It means this very unique place where we actually celebrate people who ‘started at the bottom now we're here.’ Like that's us." Rogan argued that the rags-to-riches meritocracy is a uniquely American concept that is far less prevalent, even in other parts of the Western world, and even less so beyond. DEMOCRATS FAR LESS LIKELY THAN REPUBLICANS TO PRIORITIZE PATRIOTISM AS KEY VALUE, POLL FINDS "I mean that is a celebrated thing in America, uniquely and rare." Rogan continued. "Like in England the, good luck doing that. Like, you know, there's a lot of countries where there's a literal caste system, like in India. In America, it is like one of the coolest things. If you hear about a guy, 'Oh, he grew up in a trailer park, his mom was hooked on crack, and then look at him now. He's running this company. He's got 150 employees, and he gives back to the community.’ Like, that's a great story! We love that story. We love a hardworking person who's free to pursue whatever they want to do and figures out a way to make it in life." Rogan warned that in modern times, many young Americans are being taught to see any accumulated wealth as a sign of having exploited or gamed the system unfairly. "But then kids today, they look at someone who's made it in life and has acquired wealth, and they look, 'Well, you must have stolen that,’" he warned. "Like ‘You have too much! You must somehow or another you must have taken from people. We need equity.’ And they're being told all these wacky things in school by people who have never existed in the real world!" He warned that it has serious consequences when the same young people who have climbed through academic institutions then enter actual society. "And when society doesn't align with what they've learned in the university, they're like, ‘Oh, we got to burn it all down!’" MORE AMERICANS THAN EVER NOW HAVE A POSITIVE VIEW OF SOCIALISM, NEW POLL SAYS Former National RNC spokesperson Elizabeth Pipko told Fox News Digital that many young people were being taught that capitalism "is evil." "It is an incredible disservice to so many to teach them to hate all the things that are best for them, and yet that is what our university system has become. So many are taught that capitalism is evil, when in reality the system is the best there is for anybody who wants to make it, regardless of where they come from," Pipko said. "So many are taught that America is an oppressor, and not taught about the history of the world as it came to be what we know today, proving America to actually be the freest, most empathetic, charitable, innovative, and opportunity-filled nation in human history," Pipko added. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP She continued, "So many are taught that disagreement is offensive instead of being encouraged to learn from diversity of thought and becoming stronger, more well-rounded individuals. What’s being taught in so many of our universities is not only often factually inaccurate, but its material meant to hold people back and to discourage them from living their lives to the fullest." "And considering these are young people with their whole lives ahead of them, in the United States of America, in 2026, they’re some of the luckiest people alive today. What a shame they are kept from being taught that. I hope all parents of teenagers take the time to heed Charlie Kirk’s warning and recognize that their children have far more options than they’ve been led to believe," Pipko said.
